question: Which of the following causes of malabsorption occurs with alteration of the intestinal mucosa ?:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Celiac disease" -> "immune-mediated damage to intestinal mucosa" -> "alteration of intestinal mucosa" -> "malabsorption" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Crigler-Najjar syndrome" -> "defective bilirubin metabolism" -> "jaundice" -> "no direct alteration of intestinal mucosa" -> "unlikely cause of malabsorption" -> 10%
CHAIN: "Cholestasis" -> "impaired bile flow" -> "reduced fat digestion" -> "malabsorption" -> "no direct alteration of intestinal mucosa" -> 40%
CHAIN: "Achalasia" -> "esophageal motility disorder" -> "difficulty swallowing" -> "no direct alteration of intestinal mucosa" -> "unlikely cause of malabsorption" -> 20%
enhanced_information: Celiac disease is a well-established cause of malabsorption due to immune-mediated damage to the intestinal mucosa, leading to its alteration and subsequent malabsorption. This aligns with the consensus that celiac disease directly affects the intestinal mucosa, causing malabsorption. The retrieved evidence paths support this by indicating interactions with components of the intestinal mucosa. Crigler-Najjar syndrome involves defective bilirubin metabolism and does not directly alter the intestinal mucosa, making it an unlikely cause of malabsorption. Cholestasis results in impaired bile flow and reduced fat digestion, leading to malabsorption, but it does not directly alter the intestinal mucosa. Achalasia is an esophageal motility disorder that affects swallowing and does not involve alteration of the intestinal mucosa, thus it is unlikely to cause malabsorption. Therefore, celiac disease is the most appropriate answer as it directly involves alteration of the intestinal mucosa leading to malabsorption.
analysis: Celiac disease is a well-known cause of malabsorption that occurs due to an alteration of the intestinal mucosa. It is an autoimmune disorder where ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine, specifically the villi, which are crucial for nutrient absorption. This damage results in malabsorption. The other options do not primarily involve alteration of the intestinal mucosa leading to malabsorption. Crigler-Najjar syndrome is a disorder of bilirubin metabolism, cholestasis involves bile flow obstruction, and achalasia affects the esophagus, not the intestinal mucosa.
